title: De transformatione serierum in fractiones continuas, ubi simul haec theoria non mediocriter amplificatur

deep.reconstruction:
This page reverses the earlier result. In §§5–8 Euler showed that s = 1/(b + 1/(c + 1/(d + …))) equals the alternating series 1/(𝔄𝔅) − 1/(𝔅ℭ) + 1/(ℭ𝔇) − …. The denominators come from the recurrence 𝔄 = 1, 𝔅 = b, ℭ = 𝔅c + 𝔄, 𝔇 = ℭd + 𝔅, ….

Here the problem is the converse. Take an arbitrary alternating series s = 1/α − 1/β + 1/γ − 1/δ + …. Euler remarks that every series can be put in this form, since the α, β, … may be fractional or negative. The goal is to find the partial quotients.

§10: Impose 𝔄𝔅 = α, 𝔅ℭ = β, ℭ𝔇 = γ, …. With 𝔄 = 1 this gives telescoping alternating products: 𝔅 = α, ℭ = β/α, 𝔇 = αγ/β, 𝔈 = βδ/(αγ), 𝔉 = αγε/(βδ), and so on.

§11: Invert the recurrence to get b = 𝔅 and, in general, the next index = (𝔑_{k+1} − 𝔑_{k−1})/𝔑_k.

§12: This yields b = α, c = (β−α)/α², d = α²(γ−β)/β², e = β²(δ−γ)/(α²γ²), f = α²γ²(ε−δ)/(β²δ²), g = β²δ²(ζ−ε)/(α²γ²ε²), h, i, … in the same pattern.

§13 begins clearing these fractional partial quotients by an equivalence transformation. The next pages show that the result is 1/s = α + α²/(β−α + β²/(γ−β + γ²/(δ−γ + …))). This is the classical Euler continued-fraction formula. By construction its convergents coincide with the partial sums of the series.
errors: No mathematical errors. I checked c, d, e, f and g directly from the stated 𝔄…𝔊; all agree.

Implicit gap: the construction tacitly requires every α, β, γ, … to be nonzero. If two consecutive terms are equal, a partial quotient becomes 0; this is harmless formally but not discussed. Convergence questions are not addressed either, though the convergents equal the partial sums exactly, so the continued fraction converges if and only if the series does.

ideas.what: Inverse problem: choose continued-fraction denominators so that the products of consecutive denominators equal prescribed numbers. This gives alternating telescoping products, from which the partial quotients are recovered.
ideas.modern_name: Construction of the continued fraction equivalent to a series (convergents = partial sums); Euler–Minding correspondence
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E247, 1750, and this paper E593); Minding (1869) for the general correspondence
ideas.where_published: E247 'De fractionibus continuis observationes'; E593 (Opuscula Analytica II, 1785)

ideas.what: Explicit partial quotients b = α, c = (β−α)/α², d = α²(γ−β)/β², …, later cleared by an equivalence transformation to give Euler's continued-fraction formula.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a standard, well-documented derivation of Euler's continued-fraction formula, which is widely credited to Euler. The calculations are correct and nothing on the page appears to be absent from the literature.
transcription_corrections: On p.145, in the line for 𝔉−𝔇, the '[?]' between the two formulas is a connecting word, presumably 'erit' or 'fit' by analogy with the neighbouring lines, as in '…erit f = α²γ²(ε−δ)/(β²δ²)'. The trailing '[?]' is just punctuation.
